summary: The major labels say the Supreme Court must overturn a ruling that will spark "chaos," but the guy who won it says such dire warnings are overblown.
body: The songwriter who won a landmark ruling on copyright termination is urging the U.S. Supreme Court to reject efforts by major music companies to overturn it, telling the justices there is no “emergency” and that publishers are “doing just fine.” The majors asked the high court this summer to tackle and reverse the first-ever ruling that came down in January, which said musicians can use termination to regain not just American songs but also overseas rights. They called the decision “profoundly wrong” and warned it will cause “chaos” for the music business. title: Android’s new cross-device hub is starting to roll out — just in time for Googlebooks
summary: Tasks, apps, notifications, and files can now follow you across devices.
body: TL;DR Google has started rolling out a new Continue activity hub through Google Play Services on Android 17. It introduces controls for continuing tasks and apps while sharing notifications, files, and media across devices. The rollout lands just ahead of the Googlebook launch, pushing Google’s broader cross-device vision closer to reality. Googlebooks aren’t going to be laptops meant to exist on their own, and the more interesting part promises to be what happens when you put one next to your Android phone. Google has spent months laying that groundwork, from Android 17’s Continue On task handoff to Play Services’ hooks for Googlebook setup and experiments that could turn your phone into a laptop trackpad . Now, one of the clearest pieces of that cross-device puzzle is starting to appear on phones. We’ve spotted a new “Continue activity” section rolling out through Google Play Services on a Pixel 9 running stable Android 17. It sits inside the existing Cross-device services menu alongside Call casting and Internet sharing, promising to let you “continue tasks and access apps, media, and notifications across your devices.”

The feature is currently in development and isn’t fully functional yet, but it could potentially pull fresh context from your calendar, emails, and tasks. Google appears to be gearing up to fix one of the biggest annoyances with the Gemini Daily Brief. Google has been actively expanding access to the feature, including making the Gemini Daily Brief available to free users and experimenting with quick audio briefing shortcuts . title: I don’t care about 7 years of Android updates, and you shouldn’t either
summary: Don't let the marketing fool you.
body: Credit: Pankil Shah / Android Authority Every Android phone manufacturer, be it Google, Samsung, or any other, loves to flex its seven-year OS update promise as the ultimate way to “future-proof” your purchase. But I don’t think it plays out the same way in reality. Sure, an Android phone can easily last six or seven years — that part isn’t in question. The real problem is that these longer updates mean nothing without new features, and even less if they just slow the phone down. That’s the part that companies obviously don’t talk about, but it’s what I want to discuss right now.

title: This upcoming flagship could react to taps and tilts faster than ever
summary: Raising the bar for touch and motion responsiveness.
body: TL;DR The OnePlus 16 could feature a new Lingxi touch chip with a 520Hz multi-finger touch sampling rate. Its gyroscope could sample movement at 800Hz, potentially improving responsiveness and precision in racing and shooting games. OnePlus is reportedly tuning the phone with FPS game studios and esports players, but the flagship isn’t expected to be sold in North America. It’s that time of the year again. The OnePlus 15 made its official debut in China in October last year, before being rolled out globally in November. Now, with its successor likely not too far behind, leaks surrounding the OnePlus 16 are starting to pick up pace — and the latest one suggests that the upcoming flagship could be a gaming beast. We already know that the OnePlus 16 could have the thinnest bezels of any OnePlus phone , alongside a 9,000mAh battery and a true 165Hz display. That’s what makes the latest leak a lot more enticing and disappointing at the same time. The OnePlus 16 isn’t coming to the US, and if the latest leak is accurate, American buyers could be missing out on a gaming-focused flagship.

title: I’ve used Android for 15 years — but I’m ready to switch to the iPhone Duo
summary: The iPhone Duo feels like the foldable I’ve been waiting for.
body: I’ve been using some sort of Android phone for practically 15 years. As a technology journalist and enthusiast, I’ve seen the entire gamut of Symbian, Tizen, Android phones, and, yes, iPhones too. Along the way, I’ve also spent a fair amount of time with the best foldable phones on the market. I’ve even liked a few. But until now, I’ve never really bought into the hype. It’s a good idea in theory. Being able to turn a phone into a tablet when you need more screen real estate, be it for media consumption or multitasking, sounds incredible. But, so far, the hardware and software integration hasn’t quite hit the spot for me. Something always felt amiss.

title: A Galaxy S25 FE user blamed One UI for battery drain, turns out it was something entirely different
summary: A user's Galaxy S25 FE started overheating and experiencing severe drain recently. The culprit was unexpected.
body: Credit: C. Scott Brown / Android Authority TL;DR A Galaxy S25 FE user recently thought a recent One UI update was causing their phone to overheat. Digging deeper revealed a WhatsApp background service was malfunctioning. WhatsApp wasn’t at fault either, as the conflict arose from two different instances of Google Play Services. One of them was due to an unofficial spoofer — MicroG — used to run to modded YouTube apps, such as ReVanced. It’s often easy to blame the latest software updates for poor device performance, but that might not always be the case. Just like that, a user recently thought a recent One UI update was making their Galaxy S25 FE run unusually long and hot, but later discovered the culprit was something entirely unrelated. Reddit user Jabbadava recently reported “severe battery drain” and “overheating” on their Galaxy S25 FE, even while it is idle. The title mentions One UI 9 and makes the recent beta rollout for the Galaxy S25 series look like the culprit that could have detrimental effects on the device’s everyday performance.

title: Is your LG TV spying on you? The company finally responds
summary: Your TV isn't all ears, but it certainly isn't minding its business.
body: TL;DR A Gamers Nexus video raised privacy concerns about LG smart TVs, including voice recognition, Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), and data collection. LG denies that its TVs continuously record conversations, saying voice processing only starts when you activate it and that ACR uses audio fingerprinting rather than recording your screen or conversations. ACR can still collect information about viewing habits when enabled, raising broader questions about whether users truly understand what they’re consenting to during TV setup. Your TV is probably one of the last gadgets in your home you expect to worry about from a privacy standpoint. You turn it on, spend 20 minutes deciding what to watch, give up and rewatch something familiar, and eventually switch it off. At least, that’s how most of us think about it. But smart TVs are effectively giant connected computers in our living rooms, which means they can collect far more information than the old dumb TVs they replaced . That issue has been thrust back into the spotlight after a recent Gamers Nexus YouTube video raised several privacy concerns around smart TVs, with LG TVs receiving particular attention.
